beats.trigger: When do you split, and how?
beats.got: The question is when to use several agents and when to use one.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: An agent maps to a job that recurs, like a role description. That is how I think about my own team's work.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: The default is one agent, and more agents cost coordination. I find that credible.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Different access is a reason to split. That is the same logic as who may see employee data, which is my works council and DPO question.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.
beats.got: More agents don't make an answer better. I would say the same about adding more people to a committee.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.

take_homes: Start with one agent and split only when the work needs different access, different language or genuinely different views. Different access is the same question as who may see employee data.
Having an agent prepare something and a person approve it is different from the agent acting. I can take that distinction to my leadership team.
The system checks how the agents handed work over, not whether the answer is true. I keep that doubt and need a human to judge the result.

monday.move: Ask my DPO and the works council representative what we may connect an agent to before I draft anything on employee data. Then try one small agent that prepares my weekly people-metrics summary from non-personal data.
monday.who: Me, the DPO, and one HR business partner as reviewer
monday.when: Ask this week, then build once I have an answer
monday.stop_condition: If the summary needs individual employee records and there is no sign-off, I stop.
monday.blocker: The works council and DPO have not been asked yet.

misconception.why: The module is about how to build and split agents and never speaks about roles or headcount. I still think the real question is which roles agents replace first, and nothing here showed me otherwise.

one_line: Good on when not to use several agents and honest about not knowing if the answer is right, but heavy on tool steps and nothing in it about the people side.
